docs.definition: Application Programming Interface. A defined contract that lets one piece of software ask another for data or actions without knowing how it works internally.
docs.example: The weather app calls the forecast API with a city name and gets back JSON with the next seven days.

docs.definition: Hiding the messy details of how something works behind a simpler interface so you can think about what it does instead.
docs.example: You call `fs.readFile()` without caring about inodes, disk sectors, or syscalls — that is abstraction doing its job.

docs.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. The four guarantees a database transaction makes so your data does not end up half-written when something crashes.
docs.example: Postgres is ACID-compliant, so if the transfer fails halfway, neither account balance changes.

docs.definition: A family of software development approaches built around short iterations, frequent feedback, and adapting the plan as you learn, rather than specifying everything up front.
docs.example: We moved to agile and now ship every two weeks instead of once a quarter.

docs.definition: A finite, well-defined sequence of steps for solving a problem or performing a computation.
docs.example: Binary search is an algorithm that finds an item in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search range.

docs.definition: Syntax that lets you write asynchronous, promise-based code that reads top to bottom like synchronous code.
docs.example: const user = await fetchUser(id); // execution pauses here without blocking the event loop

docs.definition: The server-side part of an application: databases, business logic, authentication, and the APIs the frontend talks to.
docs.example: The backend team exposed a new /orders endpoint so the mobile app can show purchase history.

docs.definition: Spending a disproportionate amount of time debating trivial details while the genuinely hard decisions get waved through.
docs.example: The RFC for the new billing system was approved in five minutes, then we spent an hour bikeshedding the name of the config flag.

docs.definition: A way of describing how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as the input size grows, ignoring constant factors.
docs.example: Looping through every pair of items is O(n²), so it gets slow fast once the list hits a few thousand entries.

docs.definition: A release strategy where you run two identical production environments and switch traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) one, so rollback is just flipping back.
docs.example: The deploy broke checkout, so we pointed the load balancer back at blue and were fixed in thirty seconds.

docs.definition: Repetitive code that has to be written in many places with little or no variation, usually to satisfy a framework or language.
docs.example: Every new Redux slice needed forty lines of boilerplate before Redux Toolkit came along.

docs.definition: The number of team members who would have to be hit by a bus (or win the lottery) before a project stalls because nobody else knows how things work.
docs.example: Only Priya knows how the billing cron works, so our bus factor for payments is one.

docs.definition: A fast storage layer that keeps copies of frequently used data so future requests can be served without recomputing or refetching it.
docs.example: We cache the product catalog in Redis for five minutes, which cut database load by 80%.

docs.definition: Deciding when cached data is stale and must be thrown away or refreshed. Famously one of the two hard problems in computer science.
docs.example: Users kept seeing their old profile picture because the CDN cache invalidation only fired on the first upload.

docs.definition: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery (or Deployment). Automatically building and testing every change, then automatically shipping changes that pass.
docs.example: Our CI/CD pipeline runs the test suite on every PR and deploys main to production after merge.

docs.definition: A function bundled together with references to the variables from the scope where it was created, so it can still use them after that scope has finished.
docs.example: function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; } — the returned arrow function is a closure over `n`.

docs.definition: The extra latency the first time a serverless function or container handles a request, because the platform has to spin up a fresh runtime first.
docs.example: Our Lambda p99 latency spikes to 2 seconds whenever there is a cold start after a quiet period.

docs.definition: A lightweight, isolated package containing an application and everything it needs to run, sharing the host operating system kernel instead of virtualizing hardware.
docs.example: We ship the API as a container so it runs the same way on a laptop, in CI, and on Kubernetes.

docs.definition: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. A browser mechanism that uses HTTP headers to decide whether a web page on one origin may request resources from another origin.
docs.example: The fetch failed with a CORS error because the API did not send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header for our domain.

docs.definition: A task scheduled to run automatically at fixed times or intervals, named after the Unix `cron` daemon.
docs.example: A cron job at 0 3 * * * rotates the logs every night at 3 AM.

docs.definition: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations most data-driven apps perform on records.
docs.example: The admin panel is basically a CRUD interface over the users table.

docs.definition: An alternate color scheme using light text on a dark background. Also, apparently, a personality trait.
docs.example: The first issue opened on our new docs site was a request for dark mode.

docs.definition: Code that is never executed or whose result is never used, but still sits in the codebase confusing people.
docs.example: Tree shaking removed 40 KB of dead code from the bundle.

docs.definition: Delaying a function call until a certain amount of time has passed without it being triggered again, so a burst of events results in a single call.
docs.example: We debounce the search input by 300 ms so we only hit the API after the user stops typing.

docs.definition: The frustrating situation where packages require conflicting versions of the same dependency, making it hard or impossible to install or upgrade anything.
docs.example: Upgrading React meant upgrading the router, which needed a newer TypeScript, which broke the linter plugin. Classic dependency hell.

docs.definition: Passing an object the things it depends on (its dependencies) from the outside rather than having it construct them itself, which makes code easier to test and swap.
docs.example: The OrderService takes a PaymentGateway in its constructor, so in tests we inject a fake one.

docs.definition: A set of practices and a culture that merges software development and IT operations, aiming for faster, more reliable delivery through automation and shared ownership.
docs.example: Since adopting DevOps, developers own their services in production and are on the pager rotation.

docs.definition: Domain Name System. The internet's phone book, translating human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
docs.example: The site was down for an hour because someone deleted the A record during a DNS migration.

docs.definition: A popular platform for building, shipping, and running applications in containers.
docs.example: docker compose up starts Postgres, Redis, and the API with one command.

docs.definition: Don't Repeat Yourself. The principle that every piece of knowledge should have a single, authoritative representation in a system.
docs.example: Instead of copying the validation rules into three forms, we kept it DRY with a shared schema.

docs.definition: A typing style where an object's suitability is determined by the methods and properties it has, not its declared type. If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck…
docs.example: Python does not care what class you pass to len() as long as it implements __len__.

docs.definition: A problem or situation that only occurs at an extreme operating parameter, like empty input, the maximum value, or a leap second.
docs.example: The date picker crashed on February 29th — an edge case nobody tested.

docs.definition: Code that runs on servers geographically close to the user (at the CDN edge) rather than in a single central region, reducing latency.
docs.example: We moved the A/B test assignment into an edge function so the right variant is chosen before the page even loads.

docs.definition: A named value set outside a program that the program can read at runtime, commonly used for configuration and secrets.
docs.example: Set DATABASE_URL as an environment variable instead of hardcoding the connection string.

docs.definition: The mechanism in JavaScript runtimes that repeatedly picks tasks off a queue and runs them, enabling non-blocking I/O on a single thread.
docs.example: A long synchronous loop blocks the event loop, so no click handlers run until it finishes.

docs.definition: A consistency model where, if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually return the same value — but reads may be stale in the meantime.
docs.example: Your like count might differ between devices for a second because the counter service is eventually consistent.

docs.definition: A switch in code that turns functionality on or off at runtime without deploying, often per user or percentage of traffic.
docs.example: The new checkout is behind a feature flag, enabled for 5% of users while we watch error rates.

docs.definition: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code changes, usually due to timing, ordering, or shared state.
docs.example: Just re-run CI, the login test is flaky on Tuesdays.

docs.definition: A feature or API that makes it easy to shoot yourself in the foot.
docs.example: Mutable default arguments in Python are a classic footgun.

docs.definition: A personal copy of someone else's repository that you can change freely, often used to propose changes back via pull requests.
docs.example: I forked the library, fixed the bug, and opened a PR upstream.

docs.definition: The part of an application users see and interact with directly, typically running in the browser or on a device.
docs.example: The frontend calls the API and renders the results as cards.

docs.definition: Automatic memory management where the runtime finds memory that is no longer reachable and frees it for you.
docs.example: The JVM paused for 400 ms during a full garbage collection, causing a latency spike.

docs.definition: A distributed version control system that tracks changes to files and lets many people collaborate on the same codebase.
docs.example: git log --oneline shows the commit history in a compact list.

docs.definition: A Git command that shows who last modified each line of a file, and when. Usually used to discover the culprit was you.
docs.example: I ran git blame on the cursed function and it was me, eight months ago.

docs.definition: A query language for APIs that lets clients request exactly the fields they need in a single request, described by a typed schema.
docs.example: The mobile app uses GraphQL to fetch a user, their last five orders, and each order's items in one round trip.

docs.definition: A high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google that uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for compact, strongly typed service-to-service communication.
docs.example: Our internal services talk gRPC, but the public API is still REST.

docs.definition: An event where people build software projects in a short, intense period — usually fueled by pizza and questionable sleep.
docs.example: The internal search tool started as a 48-hour hackathon project.

docs.definition: The default scenario where everything goes right: valid input, no errors, no edge cases.
docs.example: The demo only covered the happy path, so nobody noticed it crashes when the cart is empty.

docs.definition: A function that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value, ideally spreading inputs uniformly and making collisions rare.
docs.example: We store passwords using a slow hash function like bcrypt, never plain SHA-256.

docs.definition: A bug that disappears or changes behavior when you try to observe or debug it.
docs.example: Adding a console.log fixed the race condition, which makes it a textbook heisenbug.

docs.definition: Updating a running application with code changes instantly, without a full restart and ideally without losing state.
docs.example: With hot reload I can tweak the button padding and see it change without re-entering the form.

docs.definition: The process where client-side JavaScript attaches event handlers and state to HTML that was already rendered on the server.
docs.example: The page looks ready, but buttons do nothing until hydration finishes.

docs.definition: An operation that produces the same result no matter how many times you perform it.
docs.example: PUT /users/42 is idempotent, so retrying it after a timeout is safe.

docs.definition: Unable to be changed after it is created. To "modify" an immutable value you create a new one instead.
docs.example: Strings are immutable in Java, so concatenation builds a new string each time.

docs.definition: The persistent feeling that you are not as competent as others think and will eventually be "found out," despite evidence to the contrary.
docs.example: Ten years in and I still get imposter syndrome every time I open a Kubernetes manifest.

docs.definition: Managing and provisioning servers, networks, and cloud resources through machine-readable configuration files instead of manual setup.
docs.example: All of our AWS resources are defined in Terraform, so recreating staging is a single apply.

docs.definition: JavaScript Object Notation. A lightweight, human-readable text format for structured data, used almost everywhere APIs exist.
docs.example: {"name": "Ada", "languages": ["Python", "Rust"]}

docs.definition: JSON Web Token. A compact, signed token containing claims (like a user ID and expiry) that a server can verify without looking anything up.
docs.example: The API reads the user ID from the JWT in the Authorization header.

docs.definition: An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across a cluster of machines.
docs.example: Kubernetes restarted the crashed pod and moved it to a healthy node before anyone noticed.

docs.definition: The time delay between a request being made and the response starting to arrive.
docs.example: Moving the database to the same region as the app cut latency from 180 ms to 12 ms.

docs.definition: Deferring the loading of a resource until it is actually needed.
docs.example: Images below the fold are lazy loaded, so the initial page weight dropped by half.

docs.definition: Old code that is still in use, usually without tests, documentation, or anyone who remembers why it works.
docs.example: The invoicing module is legacy code written in 2009, and everyone is scared to touch it.

docs.definition: A tool that analyzes source code for likely bugs, stylistic problems, and suspicious patterns without running it.
docs.example: The linter caught an unused variable and a missing await before the code was even committed.

docs.definition: A component that distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to improve throughput and availability.
docs.example: The load balancer health check took the bad instance out of rotation automatically.

docs.definition: The hostname that refers to the current machine, usually resolving to 127.0.0.1. The only server guaranteed to work in your demos.
docs.example: It works on localhost:3000, so it must be a production problem.

docs.definition: A raw numeric literal in code with no explanation of what it means or why it has that value.
docs.example: Replace `if (status === 7)` with a named constant like ORDER_SHIPPED so nobody has to guess.

docs.definition: Caching the results of a function call based on its inputs so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly.
docs.example: useMemo memoizes the filtered list so it is not recalculated on every render.

docs.definition: When a program keeps holding on to memory it no longer needs, so its memory usage grows over time until something breaks.
docs.example: The dashboard tab grew to 3 GB because we never removed the scroll event listeners.

docs.definition: What Git reports when two branches changed the same lines differently and it cannot decide which version to keep.
docs.example: Two of us renamed the same function on separate branches and got a merge conflict in twelve files.

docs.definition: An architecture where an application is built as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each owning a specific business capability.
docs.example: We split the monolith into microservices, and now we have 40 services and one very tired platform team.

docs.definition: Code that sits between a request and the final handler, able to inspect, modify, or short-circuit it — often used for auth, logging, and parsing.
docs.example: The auth middleware rejects requests without a valid session before they reach the route handler.

docs.definition: A single version-controlled repository that holds many projects or packages, often with shared tooling.
docs.example: The web app, mobile app, and shared UI library all live in one monorepo managed with pnpm workspaces.

docs.definition: Minimum Viable Product. The smallest version of a product that can be released to learn whether it solves a real problem.
docs.example: The MVP was a Google Form and a spreadsheet, and it got us our first ten paying customers.

docs.definition: A performance issue where code runs one query to fetch a list, then one additional query per item in that list, instead of fetching everything at once.
docs.example: Rendering 100 posts triggered 101 queries because each post loaded its author separately.

docs.definition: Presenting someone with a problem so interesting that they cannot help dropping everything to solve it.
docs.example: I asked in Slack why our build was 3 seconds slower on Mondays and nerd sniped half the platform team.

docs.definition: An error raised when code tries to use a reference that points to nothing.
docs.example: The app crashed with a NullPointerException because the user had no profile picture.

docs.definition: How well you can understand a system's internal state from its external outputs — logs, metrics, and traces.
docs.example: Better observability meant we found the slow query from a single trace instead of guessing for a day.

docs.definition: A logic error where a loop or calculation goes one step too far or stops one step short.
docs.example: for (let i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++) reads one element past the end — a classic off-by-one error.

docs.definition: A rotation where an engineer is responsible for responding to production incidents outside normal hours.
docs.example: I am on-call this week, so my phone stays on loud even at the movies.

docs.definition: Software whose source code is publicly available under a license that lets anyone use, study, modify, and distribute it.
docs.example: DevTerms is open source, so you can send a pull request if you find a bug.

docs.definition: Object-Relational Mapper. A library that maps database tables to objects in your programming language so you can query without writing raw SQL.
docs.example: With the ORM, `db.query.users.findFirst()` replaces a hand-written SELECT.

docs.definition: Splitting a large result set into smaller pages that are fetched one at a time.
docs.example: The API returns 20 results per page and a cursor for the next page.

docs.definition: Two developers working together at one workstation: one writes code (the driver) while the other reviews and guides (the navigator).
docs.example: We pair programmed the migration so two people understood every step.

docs.definition: Code that implements a modern feature in older environments that do not support it natively.
docs.example: We added a polyfill for structuredClone so the app still works on older Safari.

docs.definition: The live environment where real users interact with your software. Also known as "where the real testing happens."
docs.example: Never run migrations against production on a Friday afternoon.

docs.definition: A request to merge changes from one branch into another, typically accompanied by code review and automated checks.
docs.example: Open a pull request and tag someone from the payments team for review.

docs.definition: A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing or ordering of concurrent operations.
docs.example: Two requests read the stock count at the same time and both sold the last item.

docs.definition: Restricting how many requests a client can make in a given time window, to protect a service from abuse or overload.
docs.example: The API returns 429 Too Many Requests after 100 calls per minute.

docs.definition: A file at the root of a project explaining what it is, how to install it, and how to use it. Frequently out of date.
docs.example: The README says to run `make setup`, but the Makefile was deleted two years ago.

docs.definition: Restructuring existing code to improve its design or readability without changing its external behavior.
docs.example: We refactored the 900-line component into five smaller ones, and all the tests still pass.

docs.definition: Regular expression. A compact pattern language for matching text — and for creating new problems.
docs.example: /^\d{3}-\d{4}$/ matches strings like 555-1234.

docs.definition: A bug where something that used to work stops working after a change.
docs.example: The dark mode regression was caused by a CSS variable rename in the last release.

docs.definition: Representational State Transfer. An architectural style for web APIs using standard HTTP methods on resources identified by URLs.
docs.example: GET /articles/12 fetches an article; DELETE /articles/12 removes it.

docs.definition: Reverting a system to a previous known-good state, usually after a bad deploy.
docs.example: Error rates doubled after the release, so we triggered a rollback within ten minutes.

docs.definition: Explaining your code line by line to an inanimate object (classically a rubber duck), which often makes you spot the bug yourself.
docs.example: I was halfway through explaining the bug to the duck on my desk when I realized I had swapped the arguments.

docs.definition: The gradual, uncontrolled expansion of a project's requirements after it has started.
docs.example: It started as "add a CSV export" and three weeks later we were building a full reporting dashboard. Scope creep.

docs.definition: Software Development Kit. A bundle of libraries, tools, and documentation for building software against a particular platform or service.
docs.example: The Stripe SDK wraps the REST API so you can call stripe.customers.create() directly.

docs.definition: A versioning scheme of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where major bumps signal breaking changes, minor adds features, and patch fixes bugs.
docs.example: Going from 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 tells users to read the migration guide before upgrading.

docs.definition: A cloud model where you deploy functions or apps without managing servers; the provider handles scaling and you pay per use. There are still servers.
docs.example: The image resizer runs serverless and costs us about four dollars a month.

docs.definition: A browser feature that lets a component attach an encapsulated DOM tree whose styles and markup are isolated from the rest of the page.
docs.example: The video player uses Shadow DOM, so our global CSS cannot accidentally restyle its controls.

docs.definition: Moving testing, security, and quality checks earlier in the development process instead of leaving them until the end.
docs.example: We shifted security left by running dependency scans on every pull request.

docs.definition: A design pattern that restricts a class to a single instance and provides a global point of access to it.
docs.example: The database client is a singleton so the app reuses one connection pool.

docs.definition: Code with tangled, hard-to-follow control flow and dependencies, like a plate of spaghetti.
docs.example: The checkout page is spaghetti code: four nested callbacks, global variables, and a GOTO in a comment.

docs.definition: An attack where untrusted input is inserted into a database query, letting the attacker read or modify data they should not.
docs.example: Concatenating the search term straight into the WHERE clause left the endpoint open to SQL injection.

docs.definition: Server-Side Rendering. Generating a page's HTML on the server for each request, so users and crawlers get content before JavaScript runs.
docs.example: With SSR, the product page shows up instantly even on slow phones.

docs.definition: A Q&A site where developers find answers to programming questions. Also an error caused by too much recursion.
docs.example: I copied the answer from Stack Overflow, and it was from 2011, and it was the question asker's own broken code.

docs.definition: A report of the active function calls at the moment an error occurred, used to find where and why it happened.
docs.example: The stack trace pointed straight to line 42 of parser.ts.

docs.definition: A pre-production environment that mirrors production as closely as possible, used for final testing.
docs.example: Works on staging, broke on production. Staging had a different Node version.

docs.definition: The implied future cost of choosing a quick or easy solution now instead of a better approach that would take longer.
docs.example: We shipped the hack to hit the launch date, but now that technical debt is slowing down every feature.

docs.definition: Limiting how often a function can run, so it executes at most once per time interval no matter how often it is triggered.
docs.example: We throttle the scroll handler to once every 100 ms.

docs.definition: A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript, adding static types to catch errors before runtime.
docs.example: TypeScript flagged that `user.adress` does not exist before I even saved the file.

docs.definition: An automated test that checks a small, isolated piece of code — usually a single function or class — in isolation from the rest of the system.
docs.example: The unit test for formatPrice() checks rounding, negative numbers, and currency symbols.

docs.definition: Being so dependent on one provider's proprietary services that switching becomes prohibitively expensive.
docs.example: Our whole backend is built on DynamoDB streams and Step Functions, so moving off AWS is not happening.

docs.definition: An in-memory representation of the UI that a framework diffs against the previous version to compute the minimal set of real DOM updates.
docs.example: React compares the new virtual DOM to the old one and only touches the list item that changed.

docs.definition: A portable binary instruction format that runs in browsers at near-native speed, letting languages like Rust and C++ target the web.
docs.example: Figma compiles its C++ rendering engine to WebAssembly.

docs.definition: An HTTP callback: a URL you give a service so it can notify you by sending a request when an event happens.
docs.example: Stripe sends a webhook to /api/stripe when a payment succeeds.

docs.definition: A protocol providing a persistent, two-way connection between a client and server over a single TCP connection.
docs.example: The chat app uses a WebSocket so new messages appear instantly without polling.

docs.definition: The classic developer response when code fails elsewhere but runs fine locally.
docs.example: "The build is failing in CI." "Weird, works on my machine."

docs.definition: Cross-Site Scripting. A vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious scripts into pages viewed by other users.
docs.example: Rendering user bios as raw HTML let someone inject a script that stole session cookies. That is XSS.

docs.definition: You Aren't Gonna Need It. The principle of not adding functionality until it is actually necessary.
docs.example: I wanted to make the exporter support twelve formats, but YAGNI — we only need CSV.

docs.definition: YAML Ain't Markup Language. A human-friendly data serialization format that relies on indentation, used heavily for config files.
docs.example: One wrong indent in the YAML file and the whole deployment silently skipped the env vars.

docs.definition: A seemingly endless chain of small tasks you must complete before you can get to the thing you actually wanted to do.
docs.example: I wanted to fix a typo, but first I had to update Node, which broke the lockfile, which needed a new pnpm… four hours of yak shaving.

docs.definition: A software vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor or has no patch available, giving defenders "zero days" to fix it.
docs.example: The Log4Shell zero-day had every team scanning their dependencies over the weekend.

docs.definition: A process that has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not read its exit status.
docs.example: ps showed dozens of <defunct> zombie processes because the worker never called wait().

docs.definition: A mythical developer who is supposedly ten times as productive as their peers. Often spotted refusing to write documentation.
docs.example: He calls himself a 10x engineer, but every one of his PRs needs ten reviewers.

docs.definition: A naming convention where words are lowercase and separated by hyphens, like skewers through words.
docs.example: CSS class names like `primary-button-large` are written in kebab case.

docs.definition: A naming convention where each word after the first starts with a capital letter, with no spaces or separators.
docs.example: JavaScript variables are usually camel case: `userProfileImage`.

docs.definition: The original repository or project that your fork or dependency is derived from; changes "flow downstream" from it.
docs.example: The bug was fixed upstream, so we just need to bump the package version.

docs.definition: Building software mostly by prompting an AI model and accepting what it produces, steering by feel rather than reading every line.
docs.example: I vibe coded the landing page in an afternoon, then spent two days figuring out why the form never submits.

docs.definition: Looks Good To Me. A code review approval, sometimes given after reading the PR thoroughly.
docs.example: Reviewer left "LGTM 🚀" on a 2,000-line PR four minutes after it was opened.

docs.definition: Short for nitpick. A minor, non-blocking code review comment, usually about style or naming.
docs.example: nit: could we call this `isEnabled` instead of `enabledFlag`?

docs.definition: Crafting and iterating on the instructions given to a language model to get more reliable, useful outputs.
docs.example: A bit of prompt engineering — adding examples and a strict output format — cut our parsing errors to almost zero.

docs.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. A technique where relevant documents are fetched from a search index and added to an LLM prompt so its answers are grounded in that data.
docs.example: Our support bot uses RAG over the help center so it cites actual articles instead of making things up.

docs.definition: When an AI model confidently produces information that is false or made up.
docs.example: The model hallucinated an npm package called `react-auto-form-magic` that does not exist.

docs.definition: A program that takes no input and prints an exact copy of its own source code.
docs.example: Writing a quine in Python is a fun exercise in string formatting.

docs.definition: Describes a system that can simulate any Turing machine — meaning, given enough time and memory, it can compute anything computable.
docs.example: Even Magic: The Gathering and PowerPoint animations have been shown to be Turing complete.

docs.definition: The thing that is "just a simple endpoint" until you have to version it.
docs.example: PM: "Can you add a quick API for the partners?" Me, six months later, maintaining v1, v2 and v2-beta.

docs.definition: A tool that lets you take "works on my machine" and ship the machine.
docs.example: Instead of fixing the env issue we just put the whole thing in Docker.

docs.definition: An incredibly powerful way to turn a single small web app into 3,000 lines of YAML.
docs.example: We needed to host a blog, so naturally we set up Kubernetes.

docs.definition: Write-only code. Easy to write, impossible to read back a week later.
docs.example: Nobody knows what ^(?:[a-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+)*$ does anymore, but we are afraid to delete it.

docs.definition: Every shortcut you took to hit a deadline, accruing interest in the form of weekend incidents.
docs.example: The interest on our technical debt is now paid in on-call pages.

docs.definition: Turning function calls into network calls, and bugs into distributed bugs.
docs.example: Our microservices architecture means a typo in one service takes down six others.

docs.definition: Someone else's servers, billed by the millisecond.
docs.example: Serverless was cheap until the infinite retry loop ran all weekend.

docs.definition: There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors.
docs.example: Every incident postmortem this quarter ended with "root cause: cache invalidation."

docs.definition: The final boss. The only environment with real data, real traffic, and none of your debug tools.
docs.example: Of course the bug only happens in production.

docs.definition: A time machine for code that you will mostly use to say "git push --force" and regret it.
docs.example: I know three Git commands and I am afraid of the other 150.

docs.definition: When a function remembers where it came from, even after it has moved out.
docs.example: The click handler is a closure, so it still sees the old value of `count` from the render it was created in.

docs.definition: Code that makes money.
docs.example: The legacy code is ugly, but it processes $2M a day, so be careful.

docs.definition: A configuration format where whitespace is load-bearing and "no" means false. Sorry, Norway.
docs.example: country: NO got parsed as country: false and broke the Norwegian storefront.

docs.definition: Where you go to find out your question was closed as a duplicate of a different question.
docs.example: Marked as duplicate. The linked question is about PHP. I am writing Go.

docs.definition: JavaScript that argues back.
docs.example: TypeScript is telling me `undefined` is not assignable to `string`, and honestly it has a point.

docs.definition: Minimum Valuable Prototype. Shipped with the understanding it will be rewritten, then never rewritten.
docs.example: The MVP from 2019 is still running the entire signup flow.

docs.definition: The phase where the page looks interactive but secretly is not yet. Also the reason for half of all React console warnings.
